newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ICE HOCKEY-CZECH COACH BUKAC RESIGNS DUE TO PLAYER RIFT.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-CZECH COACH BUKAC RESIGNS DUE TO PLAYER RIFT.

text.p: Czech National ice hockey team coach Ludek Bukac on Friday said he was resigning from his position, following a widening rift between himself and several key players.

Since becoming coach of the national team in 1994, Bukac has driven out many top players, but also guided the Czechs last year to their first world championship since the former Czechoslovakia won the last of its six titles in 1985.

In recent weeks, he has come under intense criticism from media and players such as National Hockey League goal scoring leader Jaromir Jagr, and top Czech Extraliga goaltender Roman Cechmanek who have said they will never again play for Bukac, branding him arrogant, incompetent and dishonest.
"For me there was no alternative," Bukac told a news conference. "I can take strong criticism, but I will not let people continuously attack me."
He said that this included many journalists who criticsed his nearly every move he made after the championships.
The loss of Bukac comes at a critical time for the Czechs as they prepare to defend their world title this spring in Helsinki.
Since winning in Vienna, last year's champions have come out on top in only three of the 18 games they have played, including an embarrassing 7-1 loss to Germany as they crashed out of the World Cup.
"I don't want to believe it, but unfortunately there's nothing more I can do," said Karel Gut, Chariman of the Czech Ice Hockey federation.
Bukac's assistant Zdenek Uher will take over in the interim, and Gut said it was too early to speculate over who may end up being his permanent replacement.

After the national team's pitiful performance at last month's Sweden Cup where they finished last, losing three out of four games, Veteran defenceman Drahomir Kadlec said he was humiliated by the experience.

The 31-year-old defenceman, who was a second team all-star at last year's world championships, complained Bukac gave the players almost no instruction on the ice in Sweden, and then shirked responsibility for the team's poor performance.
"No one told us what to do during the games," he said, "and when we lost, the coaches didn't accept any responsibility. They looked for excuses."
At the end of the Swedish tournament, Bukac told reporters that his players had not been prepared mentally or physically, and he criticised their performance at both ends of the ice.
None of the players who said they would never play for Bukac again were immediately available for comment on whether they were considering returning to the national team.
